entry.title: When floods team up: what 378 studies tell us about compound flooding

link.title: When floods team up: what 378 studies tell us about compound flooding

entry.content:
We usually think of floods one at a time: a river overflows, a downpour overwhelms city drains, or a storm pushes the sea onto the coast. In reality, the worst floods often come when several of these happen at once. When Hurricane Harvey struck Texas in 2017, extreme rainfall, high rivers and storm surge combined. Scientists call such events compound floods.

A new systematic review in Environmental Impact Assessment Review by Usman Mohseni, R. Vinnarasi, Abdou Khouakhi and Amir AghaKouchak, published online in July 2026, brings together 378 studies of compound flooding from 1961 to 2025 (Mohseni et al. 2027). It asks three questions: what drives compound floods, how we model them, and where research should go next. This post is the second this week involving AghaKouchak’s group; the first looked at how one drought can set off a chain of other hazards.

1. Three main drivers, and many helpers

The review finds that most compound floods involve three main drivers:

  • Heavy rain (pluvial flooding), which overwhelms drains and fills streets, especially in cities with sealed surfaces.
  • High river flow (fluvial flooding), from long or intense rain, snowmelt or dam releases.
  • Storm surge (coastal flooding), the rise of the sea pushed by strong winds and low pressure in storms.

The danger lies in how they interact. A high sea can block a river from draining into it, so the river backs up and floods inland. A high tide can stop city drains from emptying, so even moderate rain floods the streets. Soils that are already wet from earlier rain cannot absorb more, so the next downpour runs straight off.

Many secondary factors make things worse: high tides, waves, sea-level rise, sinking land in deltas and coastal cities, rising groundwater, snowmelt, ice jams, and human structures such as levees and drains that work well for one hazard but can shift the risk elsewhere.

2. Why “together” changes the odds

The key point is that the combined flood can be much worse, and much more likely, than each driver alone would suggest. Figure 1 shows a simple example. Suppose heavy rain and storm surge each reach their 10-year level. If the two were completely independent, both would happen together only once in about 100 years. But they are often not independent, because the same storm brings both the rain and the surge. With a modest link between them, the combined event becomes a once-in-about-46-years event, and with a stronger link, once in about 26 years.

Figure 1. How often two 10-year events happen together depends on how strongly they are linked. With no link (independence), the joint event happens once in about 100 years; with a correlation of 0.6, once in about 26 years. Figure by Daeha Kim, a simple illustration using a standard statistical model (a Gaussian copula), not taken from the review.

This is why the review stresses that ignoring the dependence between drivers leads to underestimating flood risk. A design that assumes independence may protect a coastal city far less well than its engineers think.

3. How we model compound floods

The review groups the 378 studies by their main method:

  • Statistical models (53% of studies) estimate how often drivers occur together, often with copulas, a family of tools that describe how two or more variables move together. They are fast and need little data, but they say nothing about where the water goes.
  • Numerical models (42%) simulate the physics of water flowing over land, in rivers and along coasts. They show which streets flood and how deep, but they are slow and need detailed data.
  • Hybrid models (5%) combine the two, for example by using statistics to choose realistic storm scenarios and a physical model to simulate them, or by training machine learning to mimic a slow physical model. They are still rare but growing quickly since about 2019.

The review also highlights a growing problem: non-stationarity. Traditional flood statistics assume that the past is a good guide to the future. With rising seas, sinking land, more intense rain and expanding cities, that assumption no longer holds, and even the link between drivers may change over time. Only a small share of studies so far take this into account.

4. What the research is about, and where it comes from

Research on compound flooding has exploded. Fewer than 20 studies appeared between 1961 and 2000, but more than 230, over 60% of the total, were published in just 2021–2025. Yet the focus is uneven (Figure 2).

Figure 2. (a) Main research focus of the 378 reviewed studies and (b) the five countries with the most studies. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Mohseni et al. (2027).

Most studies develop methods or analyze the hazard itself. Far fewer assess the actual impacts on people and property (5%) or try to forecast compound floods in real time (4%). Geographically, the USA alone accounts for nearly a third of the studies, followed by China and the UK. Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, where many people live in exposed coastal deltas and cities, remain largely unstudied.

5. Where research should go next

The authors propose several directions:

  1. Use more and better data, from satellites, weather reanalyses, sensors and even crowdsourcing and social media, to describe floods where gauges are scarce.
  2. Build models that allow change over time, linking the behavior of flood drivers to factors such as sea-level rise, land use and climate patterns like El Niño.
  3. Create libraries of flood maps for compound events. Such libraries exist for river floods, so that forecasters can quickly look up the expected flooding, but not yet for compound floods.
  4. Explore many scenarios, not just one, to deal with the deep uncertainty about future climate and cities.
  5. Connect the physics with people, including exposure, vulnerability and how human decisions shape flood risk.
  6. Close the regional gaps, especially in the most vulnerable parts of the world.

6. Why this matters for Korea

Korea has a long coastline, large tidal ranges on the west coast, and typhoons that bring heavy rain and storm surge at the same time. Many cities, such as Busan, Incheon and Changwon, sit where rivers meet the sea. The review lists Korea among the countries with a moderate number of compound flood studies, so there is a base to build on. As sea levels rise and summer rainfall intensifies, flood planning that treats rain, rivers and the sea separately may increasingly underestimate the risk.

Questions to think about

  1. Why might the same storm make both heavy rain and storm surge more likely? What does that do to the chance of a compound flood?
  2. Think of a coastal city you know. Where do its rivers and drains meet the sea, and what happens to them at high tide?
  3. A levee may protect against river floods but trap rainwater behind it. How should engineers design for more than one driver at once?

Reference

Mohseni, U., Vinnarasi, R., Khouakhi, A., & AghaKouchak, A. (2027). A systematic review of compound flooding: drivers, models, and future directions. Environmental Impact Assessment Review, 122, 108620. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eiar.2026.108620

The figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1 and Figure 2.

entry.title: Beyond the drought map: monitoring what drought actually does

link.title: Beyond the drought map: monitoring what drought actually does

entry.content:
Drought monitoring has come a long way. A century ago, it meant counting the days without rain at a few weather stations. Today, satellites measure rainfall, soil moisture, vegetation, snow and even the total water stored underground, and drought maps are updated every week. Yet a Perspective in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment by Amir AghaKouchak and 21 colleagues argues that these maps still answer the wrong question (AghaKouchak et al. 2023). They tell us how dry it is. What farmers, water managers and emergency planners need to know is what the drought will do.

1. Seventy indicators, one blind spot

The authors count more than 70 drought indicators. Some use a single variable, such as the Standardized Precipitation Index for rainfall or soil moisture percentiles. Others combine several variables into one composite index. Operational systems, such as the US Drought Monitor, blend many of these with the judgment of hundreds of local experts.

This variety exists for a good reason: drought is not one thing. A shortage of rain (meteorological drought) can lead to dry soils (agricultural drought), which can lead to low rivers, reservoirs and groundwater (hydrological drought), each on its own timescale. Snow adds another layer. In many mountain regions, the snowpack is the largest natural reservoir, and a “snow drought” can occur even after a normal winter if warm weather melts the snow too early.

But all of these indicators share one feature: they describe the hazard, not its consequences. They are “top-down”. A map can show that soil moisture is two standard deviations below normal, but not whether this means a 10% or a 50% loss of wheat yield, a water shortage in a city, or a fire season ahead.

2. Droughts rarely come alone

The second problem is that droughts are monitored in isolation, while in reality they set off chains of other hazards (Figure, panel a). The authors call these cascading hazards:

  • Heatwaves. When soils dry out, less of the sun’s energy goes into evaporating water and more goes into heating the air. Drought and heat then feed each other. The 2003 European drought and heatwave is estimated to have killed more than 70,000 people.
  • Wildfires. Drought dries out vegetation and turns it into fuel. Several years of drought preceded the extreme fire seasons in Australia and the western USA in 2020.
  • Debris flows. Drought weakens soils and opens deep cracks, and fire removes the vegetation that holds slopes together. When intense rain then falls on burned slopes, mud and boulders can rush downhill. In Montecito, California, a drought from 2012 to 2016 was followed by a large fire in December 2017 and, a month later, by intense rain that triggered the deadliest debris flow in the state’s history.
  • Floods. Droughts and floods are two ends of the same water cycle, and droughts can make floods worse. Cracked soils can weaken levees: during the dry summer of 2003, a dyke failed at Wilnis in the Netherlands, flooding about 600 homes. California’s 2012–16 drought ended with extreme rain that badly damaged the spillway of the Oroville Dam, and Australia’s Millennium Drought ended in 2011 with widespread flooding.
  • Water quality. Low river flows mean less dilution and warmer water, which encourage algal blooms. The authors link drought to the dead zone in Lake Erie in 2012, and toxins from algae closed the water supply of Toledo, Ohio, in 2014.

Figure. (a) A drought can set off a chain of further hazards, illustrated with the Montecito, California example described by AghaKouchak et al. (2023); the timeline is not to scale. (b) The shift the authors propose, from monitoring how dry it is to forecasting what the drought will do. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on AghaKouchak et al. (2023).

None of the existing indicators captures these links. A drought index does not tell you that a wildfire is likely, and nothing tells you that the cracked soil on a burned hillside has become dangerous when the rain returns.

3. From “how dry?” to “what will it do?”

The authors’ main proposal is impact-based drought monitoring (Figure, panel b). Instead of starting from rainfall and soil moisture, it starts from the things people care about: crop yields, food prices, drinking water, hydropower, jobs, health and the risk of fire or flood. Drought information is then linked to models that translate the hazard into these impacts, ideally months in advance.

One example in the paper is snow. In many basins, irrigated wheat, rice and maize depend heavily on snowmelt. Linking a snow drought map to these farms would turn “less snow than normal” into “this much less irrigation water for these crops this summer”.

4. Why it is hard

If this is such a good idea, why is it not done already? The authors list several obstacles:

  1. Few consistent impact records. Damage from drought is slow, spread out and often unrecorded. Systems such as the US Drought Impact Reporter, which lets citizens and local officials report impacts, are a start, but such data remain patchy.
  2. Missing water-use data. The impact of a drought depends on how much water people take and where it comes from. Even in the USA, water use by sector is published only at the county level every five years. Los Angeles, for example, cannot judge its drought risk from local rainfall alone, because much of its water comes from northern California and the Colorado River.
  3. Unknown local storage. Groundwater and the water stored in lakes and reservoirs are poorly measured in much of the world, and satellite measurements of total water storage are too coarse for a single basin.
  4. Disconnected tools. Drought monitors, crop models, fire systems and flood forecasts are run by different agencies and rarely talk to each other.

5. New data and AI as part of the solution

The authors see two developments that could help. New satellites, such as SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), launched in December 2022, measure both the area and the water level of lakes and reservoirs, giving a new picture of how much water is actually stored. And with data volumes growing far beyond what people can inspect by hand, artificial intelligence, especially models that combine physical knowledge with machine learning, can help learn the complicated links between drought and its impacts.

6. What this means for us

For water researchers, the message is that a good drought index is only the first step. The next step is to connect it to what happens on the ground, and to monitor droughts together with the heatwaves, fires and floods they bring, instead of in separate silos.

This also matters for Korea. Our droughts are often short and sharp, such as flash droughts during hot summers, and they increasingly overlap with heatwaves, wildfires in spring and heavy monsoon rain. Knowing what a dry spell will do to reservoirs, farms and burned mountain slopes may be more useful than knowing that it is dry.

Questions to think about

  1. Think of the last drought in your region. What did the drought map say, and what actually happened to farms, water supplies or forests?
  2. Why might a drought end in a flood? Which processes make the transition dangerous?
  3. If you could collect one new kind of data to forecast drought impacts better, what would it be?

AghaKouchak 등(2023)은 70개가 넘는 가뭄 지수와 위성 자료로 가뭄 감시가 크게 발전했지만, 여전히 ‘얼마나 건조한가’라는 위험(hazard)만 보여줄 뿐 ‘그 가뭄이 무엇을 일으킬 것인가’라는 영향은 알려주지 못한다고 지적한다. 실제로 가뭄은 폭염, 산불, 산불 뒤 집중호우에 의한 토석류, 홍수, 수질 악화로 이어지는 연쇄 재해를 일으키는데(예: 2012–16년 가뭄, 2017년 12월 산불, 2018년 1월 토석류로 이어진 미국 캘리포니아주 몬테시토), 현재의 감시 체계는 이들을 따로따로 다룬다. 저자들은 작물 수확량, 식수, 수력발전, 일자리 같은 영향에서 출발하는 ‘영향 기반 가뭄 감시’로 전환하자고 제안하며, 이를 위해 일관된 영향 기록과 지역별 물 사용·저류량 자료, SWOT 같은 새 위성 자료, 그리고 물리 지식과 결합한 AI가 필요하다고 본다. 짧고 강한 돌발가뭄이 폭염, 봄철 산불, 장마철 호우와 겹치는 한국에서도 가뭄을 다른 재해와 함께, 그리고 그 영향 중심으로 감시할 필요가 크다.

Reference

AghaKouchak, A., Huning, L. S., Sadegh, M., Qin, Y., Markonis, Y., Vahedifard, F., et al. (2023). Toward impact-based monitoring of drought and its cascading hazards. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, 4, 582–595. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00457-2

The figure is original. The Python script that produces it is available on GitHub.
entry.summary: A Perspective by AghaKouchak and colleagues argues that drought monitoring should move from measuring how dry it is to forecasting what the drought will do, including the heatwaves, wildfires, debris flows and floods that often follow it.

entry.title: Ten years after Paris: what the 2026 Lancet Countdown says about climate and health

link.title: Ten years after Paris: what the 2026 Lancet Countdown says about climate and health

entry.content:
Every year since 2016, the year the Paris Agreement entered into force, a large international team has published a check-up on how climate change is affecting human health. The tenth report of the Lancet Countdown, written by 146 researchers and published in The Lancet in October 2026, looks back over that whole decade (Romanello et al. 2026). Its title sums up the conclusion: “a decade of escalating health harms and a decisive moment for all.”

The report is long, with 54 indicators covering heat, extreme weather, infectious disease, food, air pollution, money and politics. Here I pick out the main messages, with a focus on the water-related ones that matter most to hydrologists.

1. Not only worse, but getting worse faster

The most striking finding is about speed. Comparing the ten years after Paris (2016–25) with the ten years before (2006–15), the report finds that many health threats have not just increased, but increased at an accelerating rate (Figure).

Figure. Four headline indicators, before and after the Paris Agreement entered into force: (a) average heat-related deaths per year (the latest period is 2016–23), (b) heatwave days per person aged 65 and over, (c) share of global land with at least one month of extreme drought in a year, and (d) share of global land with at least one very extreme daily rainfall (rarer than once in ten years) in a year. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Romanello et al. (2026).

Heat. Heat was linked to about 540,800 deaths per year in 2016–23, up from about 398,400 per year in the previous decade. In 2023, the number reached a record of about 710,000, and the authors attribute 71.5% of those deaths to human-caused climate change. In 2025, the average person on Earth experienced 13.5 heatwave days, and 11.3 of them would not have been expected without climate change. People over 65, who are the most vulnerable, faced 11.5 heatwave days a year on average, up from 7.2.

Work and money. Heat cost 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, equivalent to about 1.07 trillion US dollars in lost income. The burden is strikingly unequal: in countries with the lowest human development the losses equal 5.0% of GDP, ten times the 0.5% in the most developed countries.

2. Water extremes: drier and wetter at the same time

For hydrologists, the drought and rainfall indicators are the most interesting part of the report.

  • Drought. In 2016–25, on average 41.7% of the world’s land experienced at least one month of extreme drought each year, up from 28.4% in 2006–15. In 2025, the figure was 51.8%, the second highest on record after 2023 (54.9%). The report measures drought in two ways: from climate data, using a standard drought index that combines rainfall and evaporation, and from GRACE satellites, which weigh changes in the water stored on and under the land.
  • Water storage. The satellite data show that between 2003 and 2025, water storage fell in about 43% of global land and rose in about 37%. Drying and wetting are happening side by side, often in neighboring regions.
  • Extreme rainfall. In 2016–25, 17.2% of global land saw at least one very extreme daily rainfall (rarer than a 1-in-10-year event) each year, up from 14.8%. The growth itself has sped up: the increase was 57% larger than in the decade before.

Droughts are the single most destructive climate hazard for agriculture, and floods bring injuries, drowning, contaminated water and waterborne disease. The report also warns that these hazards increasingly come together or one after another, so the real risk can be larger than any single indicator suggests.

3. Adaptation is lagging

Protection is not keeping pace. By 2025, about three in four WHO member states had not reported completing a health vulnerability and adaptation assessment since 2020, and about seven in ten had no health adaptation plan. International climate finance has covered less than a third of even the limited adaptation needs that developing countries have reported, and development aid is falling sharply. The report notes that aid from the 17 largest donors is projected to drop by roughly a quarter within three years, with South Korea among the countries making the largest proportional cuts.

There are bright spots. Early warning systems for climate-related health hazards now exist in 75 countries, and 56 countries have a health adaptation plan, up from 14 in 2015.

4. The fossil fuel problem, and the opportunity

Fossil fuels still supply about 81% of the world’s energy. They also harm health directly: air pollution from burning them caused about 2.78 million deaths a year on average since 2016. Meanwhile, countries spent a cumulative 6.2 trillion US dollars on net fossil fuel subsidies between 2016 and 2024, and in 2024 ten countries spent more on these subsidies than on their health systems.

But the report also documents real progress. Renewables are now cheaper than fossil power in many places, clean energy investment in 2025 exceeded fossil fuel investment by 82%, and in more than half of the 140 countries assessed, deaths from fossil fuel air pollution have fallen, saving an estimated 323,000 lives a year. Expected warming by 2100 has come down from 3.0–3.5 °C to 2.6–3.4 °C since the Paris Agreement. That is still far too high, but it shows that action works.

5. A decisive moment

The authors are frank about the politics. The USA withdrew from the Paris Agreement and WHO, climate disinformation is growing, and the 2026 war involving Iran has disrupted oil markets, pushing some countries towards renewables and others back towards fossil fuels. Against this, the report calls for six priorities, including formally recognizing climate change as a global health emergency, putting the reduction of deaths and illness at the center of all climate policy, and building a global data commons on climate and health as a public good.

That last point deserves attention from our field. Almost every indicator in this report rests on long, open records of temperature, rainfall, drought and water storage. Keeping those observations running, and openly available, is part of protecting health.

Questions to think about

  1. The report measures drought both with a climate index and with satellite water storage. Why might the two give different pictures of the same drought?
  2. Heat costs the least developed countries ten times more of their GDP than the most developed ones. What makes the same heat so much more costly in some places?
  3. Which water-related health risks in your own country are tracked well, and which have no long-term record at all?

Reference

Romanello, M., Walawender, M., Israelsson, J., Hasan, M. M., Battaglia, F., Dutta, A., et al. (2026). The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: a decade of escalating health harms and a decisive moment for all. The Lancet, 408, 1979–2032. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01779-4

entry.summary: The tenth Lancet Countdown report tracks 54 indicators of how climate change affects our health. Its message is that the harms have not only grown since the Paris Agreement, but grown faster, from deadly heat to droughts and extreme rainfall.

entry.title: Push until it breaks: why good research tells you where it fails

link.title: Push until it breaks: why good research tells you where it fails

entry.content:
Most research papers are success stories. A new method works, a model fits the data, a device performs as designed. What we rarely read is where the method stops working. A short editorial in Nature Communications argues that this silence is a missed opportunity, and asks authors to do something unusual: push their work until it breaks, and tell readers where and why (Nature Communications 2026).

1. What the editorial asks for

The message is simple. Don’t only show that your system works under expected conditions; test its boundaries. Push your assumptions, methods, models or devices until they falter, and report the point where they fail and the reason.

The editors acknowledge that testing to failure costs time and money. But they argue that the breaking points are not weaknesses to hide. They are some of the most useful information a paper can contain, because they tell others how the work can be used responsibly, and where the next advance has to come from. A paper that shows where it fails helps define the frontier of a field, instead of only adding to it.

The editorial also offers practical advice:

  • Be selective. Report the failures that matter for the main claims, and put side analyses in the supplementary material.
  • Learn from past reviews. Since November 2022, the journal has published the peer-review files of its research articles. Reading what reviewers asked for in similar work shows which limitations the community cares about.
  • Don’t fear rejection. Disclosed limitations, on their own, are not held against a paper by the editors, and reviewers are asked to take the same view.

2. Hydrologists have been saying this for forty years

This idea will be familiar to hydrologists. In 1986, Vít Klemeš proposed a hierarchy of tests for hydrological models (Klemeš 1986). The simplest, the split-sample test, calibrates a model on one part of a record and checks it on another. But if both parts come from similar climate, the test says little about how the model behaves when conditions change. Klemeš therefore proposed a tougher differential split-sample test: calibrate the model in wet years and test it in dry years, or the other way around. A model meant for a changing world should pass that test.

Two decades later, Andréassian and colleagues called for “crash tests” of hydrological models, borrowing the idea from the car industry: you learn the most about a car’s safety by deliberately driving it into a wall (Andréassian et al. 2009). When such tests were run on 216 Australian catchments, model errors grew as the climate of the test period moved further from that of the calibration period (Coron et al. 2012).

3. A toy crash test

The figure below shows a simple example. Suppose the “real” relationship between annual precipitation and runoff in a catchment follows a Budyko curve, a well-established description of how precipitation is split between evaporation and runoff. Now fit a simple straight line to years with 1,100 to 1,500 mm of precipitation.

Figure. A toy crash test. (a) “Real” annual runoff from a Budyko curve and a straight-line model fitted only to the years in the blue band. (b) The model’s error. Inside the calibration range the error is about 1%; below about 830 mm of precipitation it exceeds 20%, and in very dry years the model predicts negative runoff. Figure by Daeha Kim, an illustrative example that does not describe any real catchment.

Inside the calibration range, the model is almost perfect, with errors around 1%. A paper that tested it only there would report an excellent model. But in drier years, the error grows quickly: at 800 mm the model underestimates runoff by more than a quarter, and below about 620 mm it predicts negative runoff, which is physically impossible. The useful finding is not that the model works, but where it stops working: somewhere around 830 mm of annual precipitation.

This is exactly what the editorial asks for. Reporting that breaking point does not make the model worse. It tells users when they can trust it.

4. Why this matters more in a changing climate

For water and climate research, the stakes are high. Almost every study of climate change impacts asks a model to work under conditions it has never seen: warmer temperatures, longer droughts, more intense rainfall. In a sense, every climate projection is a differential split-sample test that we cannot run, because the future data do not exist yet. The least we can do is test our models across the widest range of past conditions available and say clearly where they began to fail.

The same applies beyond hydrology. Machine-learning models are notorious for performing brilliantly on data similar to their training set and failing on anything different. Engineering designs, statistical methods and AI tools all have edges, and users deserve to know where they are.

5. What this means in practice

For students and young researchers, the editorial suggests a few habits worth adopting:

  1. State the range of conditions you tested, for example the climates, catchment types or data periods, and avoid claims beyond it.
  2. Deliberately test the hard cases, such as the driest years, the largest floods or the most unusual catchments, even if the results look bad.
  3. Report where and why your method fails, not just that it fails. The “why” is what helps others improve it.
  4. Treat limitations as results, not as an apologetic paragraph at the end of the discussion.

It takes some courage to show where your own work breaks. But in research, as in engineering, knowing where things fail is as valuable as knowing that they work.

Questions to think about

  1. In your last model study, what was the driest or most extreme condition you tested? Would you trust the model beyond it?
  2. Why do you think papers so rarely report failures? What could reviewers and journals do to change that?
  3. If you were asked to design a “crash test” for a model in your field, what wall would you drive it into?

entry.title: Ageing pipes, ageing people: the double ageing of water infrastructure

link.title: Ageing pipes, ageing people: the double ageing of water infrastructure

entry.content:
Most of the pipes, dams, levees and treatment plants that serve us today were built in a burst after the Second World War, mostly between the 1950s and 1970s. They are now reaching the end of their design lives at about the same time. That alone is a big engineering problem. A new comment in Nature Water by Vahedifard and colleagues argues that it is only half of the problem: the people these systems serve have aged too, and planning rarely takes that into account (Vahedifard et al. 2026).

1. The first ageing: the infrastructure

The numbers the authors collect are striking:

  • In the USA, nearly a fifth of drinking-water mains, more than 724,000 km of pipe, have already passed their design life of 75–100 years.
  • In England and Wales, water mains were 57 years old on average in 2021, and 13% were more than 100 years old.
  • US levees protecting property worth over 2 trillion US dollars are 62 years old on average.
  • Large dams in the UK and Japan are, on average, more than a century old. Worldwide, more than half of large dams with a known completion date are already 50 years or older.

On top of this, infrastructure built for the climate of the twentieth century is now being asked to cope with the floods, droughts and heatwaves of the twenty-first.

2. The second ageing: the people

The postwar systems were built for young, growing societies with an expanding workforce and tax base. That is no longer the world they serve. The number of people aged 65 and over is projected to reach 1.6 billion by 2050, nearly double the 2021 level. Japan and more than twenty European countries already have a fifth to a third of their populations over 65.

South Korea is the most dramatic case (Figure 1). In 1970, when much of its modern water infrastructure was being built, only about 3% of Koreans were 65 or older. In December 2024 the share passed 20%, making Korea a “super-aged” society, and in the most rural provinces, such as Jeollanam-do, it is above 27%.

Figure 1. Share of the population aged 65 and over, 1960–2025, in five countries. The shaded band marks the post-war decades in which much of today’s water infrastructure was built. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on World Bank data (World Development Indicators, from the UN World Population Prospects).

3. When two kinds of ageing meet

The authors call the growing mismatch between a water system and the society it serves the infrastructure–society ageing gap. A water network built in the 1960s for a young, growing town may, sixty years later, serve a smaller and older population with less money, more health vulnerabilities and different needs. The pipes and the people have aged by the same number of years, but they no longer fit each other.

The gap shows up in four ways:

  1. Workforce. Experienced operators and engineers are retiring faster than they can be replaced, taking system-specific know-how with them.
  2. Health. Older people are more vulnerable when the water stops or becomes unsafe. They may find it harder to fetch bottled water, follow a boil-water notice or leave home during a flood.
  3. Money. Many utilities depend on water bills. A shrinking customer base means less money for maintenance, while pensions and healthcare compete for public budgets.
  4. Place. Older populations, the oldest pipes and the weakest utility finances tend to sit in the same places: rural, post-industrial and economically struggling regions.

4. A spiral that is hard to escape

The real danger, the authors argue, is that these four effects feed each other (Figure 2). Old pipes break more often. Unreliable service pushes younger residents to move away. The town becomes smaller and older, uses less water and pays less in water bills. The utility postpones repairs to stay solvent, and the pipes deteriorate faster. Less water use even causes its own problems: water sits longer in oversized pipes, and quality can suffer.

Figure 2. How ageing water infrastructure and an ageing, shrinking community can reinforce each other. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic of the decline spiral described by Vahedifard et al. (2026).

There is no natural way out of this loop. Without outside investment, new policies or new plans, each round makes the next one worse, and the longer it runs, the more expensive it becomes to fix.

5. Why this is a climate-risk problem

For me, the most important example in the comment is about floods. Imagine a levee that has been perfectly maintained and is structurally as good as the day it was built. When it was designed, it was assumed that residents would receive a warning and move themselves to safety within a few hours. If many of those residents are now in their eighties, some living alone and some in care homes, the protection the levee actually provides has fallen, even though the levee itself has not changed.

In other words, protection is not only a property of the structure, but also of the people’s ability to benefit from it. The same is true for droughts and heatwaves: a water outage during a heatwave is far more dangerous for older people than for younger ones. As climate extremes become more frequent, the cost of ignoring who lives behind the levee or at the end of the pipe will rise.

6. Planning for the people, not only the pipes

Major works on water infrastructure happen rarely. A water main may be replaced once every 75–100 years, and a levee raised once in a generation. Population change, by contrast, never stops. Each major intervention therefore sets the design assumptions for decades.

The authors contrast two approaches. An intervention that ignores the gap simply restores the system to its original design, as if the population were still the same. An intervention that accounts for the gap asks a different question: not just “how old is this asset?” but “who will this system serve over its lifetime?” The physical work may be similar, but the design, emergency plans, communication and financing are updated for the people who actually live there now. In ageing communities, that might mean better protection and communication for vulnerable residents during outages, more affordable pricing, and financing that does not rely solely on a shrinking customer base. In young, growing places, it means flexibility and extra capacity.

The authors call for standard indicators of this gap, an open global observatory linking population projections with infrastructure inventories and condition data, and international cooperation, raising the issue at the 2026 UN Water Conference.

For Korea, where the population is ageing faster than in almost any other major economy and ageing is most advanced in rural areas, this seems especially relevant. Flood warnings, drought responses and pipe-renewal plans all quietly assume something about who will receive them, act on them and pay for them. It may be time to make those assumptions explicit.

Questions to think about

  1. Think of a levee or dam near where you live. When it was built, who was it designed to protect, and has that population changed?
  2. If a rural water utility loses a third of its customers over the next 20 years, who should pay to keep its pipes working?
  3. How should flood warning and evacuation plans change in a town where a quarter of residents are over 65?

entry.title: Global fossil CO2 emissions set to fall in 2026, the first drop since Covid

link.title: Global fossil CO2 emissions set to fall in 2026, the first drop since Covid

entry.content:
Global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels have fallen in only a handful of years since 1960, and almost every time something had gone badly wrong with the world economy. The last time was 2020, when Covid lockdowns emptied roads and skies. According to a new estimate from Carbon Brief, 2026 may join the list: global fossil-fuel CO2 emissions are set to fall by around 0.5% this year (Evans 2026).

Half a percent sounds small, and it is. But emissions have risen in almost every year for decades, and the Global Carbon Project’s latest assessment projected a new record for 2025, about 1% higher than 2024 (Friedlingstein et al. 2026). A fall, if confirmed, would be the first since Covid and one of the few in more than 60 years.

1. What is happening

The trigger is the war between the US and Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since early 2026. Before the crisis, more than 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through the strait. The disruption sent oil and gas prices soaring. In October, Brent crude futures traded around 107 US dollars a barrel and diesel benchmarks reached all-time highs in Europe and the US (IEA 2026b).

High prices and scarce fuel have cut demand. The International Energy Agency (IEA), whose monthly oil reports are the standard reference, started the year expecting global oil demand to grow by 930,000 barrels a day in 2026. Month by month, as the crisis began and then dragged on, it revised that forecast down. By October it expected demand to fall by 2.6 million barrels a day, about 2.5%, the first annual decline since 2020 (Figure 1). Even with a partial recovery, it expects 2027 demand to remain slightly below the 2025 level (IEA 2026b).

Figure 1. The IEA’s forecast of the change in global oil demand in 2026, as published in its monthly Oil Market Reports during the year (the February value is not shown). Figure by Daeha Kim, based on IEA Oil Market Reports (2026) and Carbon Brief (Evans 2026).

2. Oil and gas down, coal up

Carbon Brief’s estimate combines the IEA’s latest forecasts for each fossil fuel (Evans 2026):

  • Oil: down about 2.4% from 2025, the main reason emissions are falling.
  • Gas: down about 0.6% already in the IEA’s July forecast, with pressure from high prices growing since.
  • Coal: up about 1.2%, instead of the small decline the IEA had expected at the start of the year.

The rise in coal has prompted headlines about a “return to coal”, and part of it is indeed a response to expensive gas. But few countries can switch from gas to coal at scale, and much of the increase has nothing to do with Hormuz. One cause will be familiar to hydrologists: a strong El Niño has raised demand for cooling and reduced hydropower output in key markets, so coal plants have filled the gap left by dry reservoirs. Another is the large amount of wind and solar power that China’s grid could not absorb earlier in the year. Overall, the extra emissions from coal are more than offset by the declines in oil and gas.

3. China leads the fall

China, the world’s largest emitter, shows the change most clearly. Its CO2 emissions fell by 3.1% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, the largest quarterly drop since the 2022 Covid lockdowns, and are now down about 0.5% for the year to date (Myllyvirta 2026). Coal use fell by 3% and oil use by 4%, with transport fuel down 9%.

What makes China different is that clean alternatives were ready. In the third quarter, generation from solar, wind and nuclear rose by 110 terawatt-hours, more than twice the growth in electricity demand. Electric vehicles reached a record 67% of passenger car sales and half of heavy-truck sales in September. China’s emissions have now been flat or falling since March 2024. Elsewhere, too, high fuel prices have pushed electric car sales to record shares, from Australia to Europe, Indonesia and Thailand, and EV sales in markets outside China, Europe and North America nearly doubled year on year in July (Evans 2026).

4. How this compares with past declines

Figure 2 shows every annual change in global fossil CO2 since 1960. Declines are rare, and nearly all of them line up with crises: the second oil shock after the Iranian revolution (1980–82), the collapse of the Soviet Union (1992), the global financial crisis (2009) and Covid-19 (2020). Each time, emissions rebounded once the economy recovered. In 2021, they jumped by almost 5%.

Figure 2. Annual change in global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and industry. Blue bars mark declines. The hatched bar is the Global Carbon Project’s projection for 2025 and the orange bar Carbon Brief’s estimate for 2026. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on Global Carbon Budget 2025 data (Friedlingstein et al. 2026, via Our World in Data) and Evans (2026).

There is a striking historical echo here. The biggest decline before 1992 also followed an oil shock linked to Iran. In 1979–80, the Iranian revolution and the Iran–Iraq war sent oil prices soaring, and global emissions fell for three years in a row. That crisis had lasting effects: it pushed countries toward nuclear power, efficiency standards and, in some places, coal, and oil never regained its earlier share of the energy mix.

5. Will it last?

That is the real question, and the honest answer is that nobody knows yet. Arguments on both sides:

Why it may be temporary. The decline is driven by a supply shock, not by climate policy. If shipping through Hormuz recovers and prices fall, oil demand is likely to bounce back, as it did after 2009 and 2020. Analysts expect Chinese oil use to rebound once prices ease (Myllyvirta 2026). Coal could also rise again if gas stays expensive into 2027.

Why it may not be. Unlike 1980 or 2020, cheap alternatives are now available at scale. A household that buys an electric car because petrol is expensive does not switch back when prices fall, and solar panels installed this year will generate for decades. “For every month the conflict lasts, the probability of permanent demand destruction increases,” as one analyst at the consultancy DNV put it (quoted in Evans 2026). The IEA, which had expected oil demand to keep growing until about 2030, now expects it to be roughly flat for two years. Governments that had planned to rely on imported liquefied gas are signaling a shift toward domestic clean energy, though some also toward keeping coal plants open longer.

Why it is not enough either way. Even a lasting decline of half a percent a year falls far short of what the Paris goals require. The UN Environment Programme estimates that global greenhouse gas emissions would need to fall by about 42% by 2030 from 2019 levels to keep 1.5°C within reach (UNEP 2024). The Global Carbon Project estimates that the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C was about 170 billion tonnes of CO2 at the start of 2026, roughly four years of current emissions (Friedlingstein et al. 2026). A peak is necessary, but it is only the first step.

6. What to watch

The Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment, usually published in November around the UN climate summit, will give the first independent full-year estimate, and final figures will only come with energy statistics next year. Until then, a few things are worth watching: whether Hormuz traffic recovers, whether the strong El Niño now developing keeps pushing up coal use and cutting hydropower, and whether the EV surge in emerging markets continues once prices fall.

Either way, 2026 is a reminder of something easy to forget: energy systems can change faster than expected when people are forced to choose. The open question is whether the world will remember the lesson when prices come down.

Questions to think about

  1. The 1970s oil shocks reshaped energy policy for decades. What policies today would turn a temporary price shock into a lasting fall in emissions?
  2. Drought and El Niño reduced hydropower and raised coal use this year. How should water resource planning account for the link between droughts and carbon emissions?
  3. If emissions fall in 2026 mainly because fuel became scarce and expensive, should it be counted as climate progress? Why or why not?

Why it is happening, how it compares with past declines, why coal is rising at the same time, and whether the drop can last.

entry.title: The AI expectations gap: what the public and AI insiders expect by 2030

link.title: The AI expectations gap: what the public and AI insiders expect by 2030

entry.content:
Ask people who build AI and people who do not what AI will be able to do in a few years, and you will get very different answers. That is not surprising. What is more interesting is why the answers differ: do the two groups hold different theories about how AI will affect work, or do they simply see different things every day?

A report published in October 2026 by Sacher, Cotter, Jones, Korinek and McCrory at the Anthropic Institute tries to answer this with two surveys run in August 2026 (Sacher et al. 2026). One reached 10,980 US adults through the polling firm Morning Consult, weighted to be nationally representative. The other was an internal poll of 1,334 Anthropic staff, people who build frontier AI and use it all day. Both groups were asked the same questions about AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how independently it will work, and what happens to workers it displaces.

One caution before the results: the report comes from an AI company and compares the public with that company’s own employees. I come back to what that means at the end.

1. Same view of today, different views of 2030

The two groups largely agree about the present. Asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level discovery, both ranked the tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty, and about a quarter of each group said AI can already design, conduct and publish a scientific study.

They part ways about the future (Figure 1a). By 2027, about 9 in 10 staff expect AI to be able to run and publish scientific studies, against 38% of the public. By 2030, 91% of staff expect AI to be capable of a Nobel-level discovery, against 39% of US adults (44% when the survey was repeated in September). Perhaps the starkest difference: depending on the task, 19 to 40% of US adults said AI will never be able to do it, compared with at most 2% of staff.

Figure 1. (a) Expectations of the US public (grey) and Anthropic staff (orange). The time-saving row compares US adults who use AI at work with staff; the last row compares employed US adults with staff and shows averages rather than shares. (b) Share expecting AI to do at least seven of eight named tasks by 2030, by experience with AI. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on data reported by Sacher et al. (2026).

The gap is not only about the frontier. Staff expect AI to be used for 65% of the work tasks it could do by 2030; the public expects 42%. Staff expect AI to work largely on its own, with people checking the result; four in ten US adults expect people to keep doing most of the work with some AI help. Asked how long a task suited to AI takes with it, including time spent checking and fixing, 59% of staff said a quarter of the time or less, compared with 26% of US adults who use AI at work. Among those workers, 29% said the task takes just as long or longer with AI, against 5% of staff.

2. Experience explains much of the gap

The most useful result, I think, is Figure 1b. Among US adults who have never used an AI tool, 28% expect AI to do at least seven of the eight tasks by 2030. Among all US adults the share is 41%, among those who use AI at work regularly (about one in five) it is 56%, and among staff it is 96%. Expectations rise with hands-on experience.

But experience does not close the gap. Even US workers in computer, engineering and science occupations who use AI regularly expect it to do only 40% of their work by 2030, closer to the average US worker (28%) than to the average staff member (75%). A frontier lab is not a typical workplace. More than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase is now written by its own AI, according to the report, and staff estimate that AI already does about half of the work of building a frontier model. People in that environment may be extrapolating from the most automatable job in the economy.

3. Same reasoning, different inputs

The two groups disagree sharply about their own jobs. On average, staff expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work hours by 2030, and over half expect at least 80%. US workers put the share at 28%, and only 1 in 20 expect 80% or more.

Yet when it comes to what this means for the labor market, the two groups reason in the same way. Respondents were told that US unemployment is about 4.2% and asked to forecast it for 2030. Among US workers, those who expect AI to do less than half of their work forecast 7 to 8%; those who expect it to do 80% or more forecast 12.2%, higher than the peak of the 2008 financial crisis. Every ten percentage points of work exposed adds about 0.4 points to the forecast, and staff at the same level of exposure give nearly the same answers. The groups do not hold different theories; they feed different inputs into the same theory.

To a hydrologist this is familiar. Two modelers can run the same rainfall–runoff model and predict very different floods simply because they use different rainfall forecasts. Arguing about the model is pointless when the disagreement lies in the forcing.

Two details complicate the picture. Staff expect AI to do most of their own work, yet 95% of them expect Anthropic’s headcount to grow over the next year, so automating tasks and shedding jobs are different predictions, at least inside a fast-growing lab. And staff are slightly more pessimistic than the public about how long a displaced worker would need to find a job in a new occupation: a median of 12 months, against 7 to 12 months for US adults.

4. What the expectations imply for the economy

The authors ran each respondent’s answers through an economic model they had published earlier, which translates beliefs about capabilities, adoption, autonomy, time savings and re-employment into GDP growth (Figure 2). The median US adult’s answers imply growth of 5.4% in 2030, already more than twice the usual US rate. The median staff member’s answers imply 17.1%, at which the economy would double in size in about four and a half years. Visitors to an online version of the quiz, self-selected and interested in AI, fell in between at 12.5%. The spread within each group is wide, and the distributions overlap.

Figure 2. Median model-implied US GDP growth in 2030 for each group, with the doubling time of GDP at that rate. Dashed lines mark the model’s Modest (2.4%), Substantial (5.4%) and Extreme (15.4%) scenarios. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on data reported by Sacher et al. (2026).

These are not forecasts by the respondents. Nobody was asked to predict GDP; the numbers are what a particular model makes of their answers. Still, the exercise shows how quickly small-sounding differences in beliefs, such as how much time a task saves, compound into very different economies.

5. Who is right?

The report does not say, and neither can I. But a few points are worth keeping in mind.

Insiders see more, but they are not neutral. Lab staff see unreleased systems and use AI more intensively than anyone, so their expectations deserve weight. They also chose to work at an AI company, which is likely to attract people who believe in the technology, and the report was produced by the same company. The authors are careful to say that staff answers are personal views, not company forecasts, but readers should still treat them as the views of an unusual group.

Other surveys find gaps in other directions. In a 2024 Pew survey, 56% of AI experts but only 17% of US adults expected AI to have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years. Yet 64% of the public expected AI to mean fewer jobs, against 39% of the experts (Pew Research Center 2025). Whether “insiders” look more optimistic or more alarming depends on who counts as an insider and what is asked.

Adoption is not capability. Even if AI can do a task, people have to choose to use it. US adults named customers preferring to deal with a person, data privacy and security, unreliable AI, and laws and liability as the biggest obstacles. Technology often spreads more slowly than its builders expect, a point I discussed in an earlier post. Not every new technology raises output much, either: one that merely replaces workers at about the same cost, a “so-so” technology in the words of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019), displaces work without adding much to GDP.

The gap may close from either side. Public expectations rise with use, so they may move toward the insiders’ as AI spreads. Or the work of a frontier lab may turn out to be unusually well suited to AI, and insiders’ expectations may come down as AI meets messier jobs. As the authors put it, how far public expectations shift will depend on whether AI comes to do as much of the work elsewhere as it does at a frontier lab.

For those of us who teach, the most practical lesson may be closer to home. The same gap exists in every classroom and research group, between people who use AI daily and people who have barely tried it. Their expectations of what students and researchers will need to know in five years differ for the same reason as in this survey: they see different things every day.

Questions to think about

  1. In your own work, what share of your hours could today’s AI do, and what share do you expect by 2030? How did using AI yourself change that estimate?
  2. The two groups reason the same way but use different inputs. In your field, is the main uncertainty about AI’s impact in the “model” or in the “forcing”?
  3. If insiders tend to overestimate and outsiders to underestimate, how would you combine their views into a single forecast?

entry.summary: A reading of a new survey comparing about 11,000 US adults with staff at a frontier AI lab: both agree on what AI can do today, but they disagree sharply about 2030, about their own jobs and about the economy, and the gap seems to come from experience rather than from different theories.

entry.title: How the brain invented learning, part VI: the future of intelligence

link.title: How the brain invented learning, part VI: the future of intelligence

entry.content:
Over five posts, this series followed the five breakthroughs of Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): steering (part I), reinforcing (part II), simulating (part III), mentalizing (part IV) and speaking (part V). The book ends with a short conclusion titled “The Sixth Breakthrough”, and the obvious candidate for that breakthrough is the one being built in data centers today.

This last post steps back. It places the five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale, looks at what AI has done in the three years since the book was written, and asks whether today’s language models are on the road to a sixth breakthrough. The first half follows the book; the second half is my own reading of developments since 2024, and it is an opinion, not a forecast.

1. Five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale

Earth scientists are used to deep time, but even for us Figure 1a is striking. The first brains appeared in the Ediacaran, about 600 million years ago. Vertebrates and their dopamine-based trial-and-error learning followed in the Cambrian, mammals and their simulating neocortex in the Jurassic, and primates near the start of the Paleogene, shortly after the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs. Speaking, which began with early humans about 2.5 million years ago, does not even get its own visible slice of the axis. It sits in the Quaternary, the thin pale band at the right end.

Figure 1. (a) The five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale (Ed Ediacaran, Cm Cambrian, O Ordovician, D Devonian, C Carboniferous, P Permian, Tr Triassic, J Jurassic, K Cretaceous, Pg Paleogene; the Silurian, Neogene and Quaternary are unlabeled). (b) The same events on a logarithmic scale of years before present, with later milestones of human culture and computing. Dates are approximate. Figure by Daeha Kim, using period boundaries from the International Chronostratigraphic Chart and the breakthroughs of Bennett (2023).

Bennett uses a calendar to make the same point, and it is worth extending. If the 600 million years since the first brains were compressed into one year, each real year would last about a twentieth of a second.

Event Years ago On a one-year calendar
First brains (steering) 600 million 1 January
Early vertebrates (reinforcing) 500 million 2 March
Early mammals (simulating) 150 million 1 October
Early primates (mentalizing) 65 million 22 November
Genus Homo (speaking begins) 2.5 million 30 December, before noon
Homo sapiens 300,000 31 December, about 7:40 pm
Writing 5,200 4.5 minutes before midnight
First electronic computers 80 4 seconds before midnight
ChatGPT 4 0.2 seconds before midnight

Figure 1b shows the same events on a logarithmic axis, which is the natural way to see a process that keeps speeding up. Each breakthrough took less time than the one before, and once language let knowledge accumulate outside individual brains, the intervals collapsed: from writing to printing to computers to language models. Whatever the sixth breakthrough turns out to be, it is happening in the last fraction of a second of Bennett’s year.

2. What Bennett means by a sixth breakthrough

In his conclusion, Bennett suggests that the next breakthrough may be intelligence that is no longer bound to biology: minds built from silicon rather than neurons, possibly far more capable than our own. His emphasis is less on when this happens than on what it inherits. Each earlier breakthrough was built from the parts of the ones before, and an artificial superintelligence would be built, at least at first, from the accumulated record of human language and the goals we choose to give it. The question he leaves the reader with is therefore partly technical and partly moral: what do we want such minds to value?

3. What has happened since the book

Bennett wrote the book when ChatGPT was new. Much has happened since, and a striking pattern is that AI seems to be acquiring rough counterparts of the five breakthroughs in a different order from evolution (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Evolution acquired the five breakthroughs in order over about 600 million years. AI systems have acquired rough counterparts of them in a different order, starting with language, within about a decade. The pairing on the right is my own interpretation, not a claim of the book. Figure by Daeha Kim.

Evolution built language last, on top of a body, a value system, a world model and a model of minds. AI started with language. Large language models were trained first to predict text (speaking). They were then tuned with human ratings of good and bad answers, a crude sense of valence (steering). By 2023 they could pass many theory-of-mind tests (mentalizing, part IV). The developments since 2024 fill in the rest.

Reinforcing returned. The biggest change since the book is the arrival of “reasoning” models, beginning with OpenAI’s o1 in September 2024. These models are trained by reinforcement learning to produce long chains of reasoning, rewarded when the final answer can be checked as correct. DeepSeek showed that this kind of training alone can make reasoning behaviors such as self-checking emerge (Guo et al. 2025). In Bennett’s terms, trial-and-error learning from part II, the oldest learning algorithm in vertebrates, was bolted onto a language model.

Results that can be checked. In July 2025, an advanced version of Google DeepMind’s Gemini solved five of the six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad, a gold-medal score certified by the competition’s coordinators and achieved in natural language within the time limit (Google DeepMind 2025a). DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve, a coding agent built on language models, found a way to multiply 4×4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on an algorithm that had stood since 1969 (Google DeepMind 2025b). The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went in part to the developers of AlphaFold.

Longer and longer tasks. METR measures the length of software tasks, timed by how long they take skilled humans, that AI agents can complete with 50% reliability. That length doubled roughly every seven months from 2019 to early 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025), and faster since. By 2026 METR noted that its measurements above 16 hours were unreliable with its current task suite, and in September 2026 it stopped updating its public chart.

Puzzles designed to resist memorization. The ARC-AGI benchmarks consist of visual puzzles that are easy for people but were built to be hard for pattern-matching systems. When the interactive ARC-AGI-3 launched in March 2026, frontier models scored under 1%. By November 2026 the best entry on the public leaderboard scored 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3 and 95.0% on ARC-AGI-2, at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per evaluation run (ARC Prize 2026).

Simulating, at last. Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 (August 2025) generates interactive environments that a user or an agent can move through in real time, keeping them consistent for a few minutes (Google DeepMind 2025c). DeepMind describes such world models as a key step toward general intelligence. This is the closest AI has come to the rat at the fork in the maze of part III.

4. Are transformers enough?

The progress is real. Whether it leads to superintelligence is a different question, and the people building these systems disagree.

One camp argues that the current recipe, large transformer models plus reinforcement learning plus more compute, will keep working. Dario Amodei of Anthropic wrote in January 2026 that AI systems as capable as “a country of geniuses in a datacenter” could be as little as one to two years away, while adding that they could also be considerably further out (Amodei 2026). I discussed the limits of the scaling side of this argument in an earlier post.

The other camp argues that something important is missing, and the missing pieces line up remarkably well with Bennett’s breakthroughs.

  • No learning from ongoing experience. Richard Sutton and David Silver argue that AI is reaching the limits of what can be learned from human data and must enter an “era of experience”, in which agents learn continually from their own interaction with the world (Silver and Sutton 2025). Andrej Karpathy has said that today’s models lack continual learning and that working agents will take about a decade. A brain never stops learning; a deployed language model mostly does. This is the plasticity of part I and the trial-and-error learning of part II, applied for a lifetime rather than during a training run.
  • No world model built from the world. Yann LeCun has long argued that predicting the next word is a dead end for human-level intelligence and that machines need world models learned from sensory data. He left Meta in late 2025 to build such systems. This is the simulating breakthrough of part III.
  • Running out of words. Villalobos et al. (2024) estimated the stock of public human text at about 300 trillion tokens and projected that, at current trends, models would use it up between 2026 and 2032. A child learns language from a tiny fraction of that (part V), because it learns from a body, a world and other people, not from text alone.

Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind sits between the camps: he has suggested that one or two more breakthroughs, in areas such as continual learning, planning and memory, may still be needed.

5. When?

Nobody knows, and the honest answer is that forecasts move. In a survey of 2,778 AI researchers conducted in 2023, the median respondent gave a 50% chance that machines would outperform humans at every task by 2047, thirteen years earlier than the same question had produced only a year before, and a 10% chance by 2027 (Grace et al. 2025). The authors of the widely read “AI 2027” scenario pushed their own estimates later in late 2025 and then earlier again in 2026; by August 2026, two of its authors, writing on the project’s blog, placed superintelligence in 2029 and 2033 respectively (Kokotajlo et al. 2025). Lab leaders tend to give the shortest timelines, and some prominent researchers, such as Karpathy, give longer ones.

As a hydrologist, I read these numbers the way I read long-range streamflow forecasts: the spread between them says more than any single value. Three observations seem robust to me.

  1. Progress is fastest where answers can be checked. Mathematics, programming and puzzles have clear right answers, so reinforcement learning works well there. Many important problems, from flood forecasting under a changing climate to policy, can only be checked slowly, partially or not at all. Expect AI to reach superhuman levels unevenly, first in verifiable domains.
  2. The missing pieces are old ones. Continual learning, grounded world models and learning from interaction are what evolution built first. Language models skipped them. Whether they can be added on top, or must be rebuilt from below, is perhaps the central question for the next decade.
  3. Values are not a detail. Bennett’s closing question, what we want these minds to want, becomes more pressing, not less, the faster the technical progress.

6. Closing

Steering took the first brains, reinforcing took a backbone, simulating took a neocortex, mentalizing took a primate brain, and speaking took a human community. Each breakthrough was slower to arrive and faster to spread than anything before it, and each was built from the parts of the last. On Bennett’s calendar, the whole story of artificial intelligence so far fits in less than a second before midnight.

I do not know whether the sixth breakthrough will come from transformers, from something that replaces them, or not for a long time. But this series has convinced me of one thing: the most useful guide to what machines are still missing is the long history of how brains got here.

Questions to think about

  1. Which of Bennett’s five breakthroughs do you think current AI systems lack most, and how would you test for it?
  2. In hydrology, which problems have answers that can be checked quickly enough for AI to learn by trial and error, and which do not?
  3. If you could choose one value or goal to pass on to a future superintelligence, what would it be, and how would you make sure it was understood as you meant it?

entry.summary: A closing note on Max Bennett's A Brief History of Intelligence: how short the age of language is on the geologic time scale, what AI has achieved since the book appeared, whether transformer-based language models can lead to a sixth breakthrough, and how uncertain the forecasts really are.

entry.title: How the brain invented learning, part V: speaking in A Brief History of Intelligence

link.title: How the brain invented learning, part V: speaking in A Brief History of Intelligence

entry.content:
This is the last part of a series on Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023). Bilaterian worms learned to steer (part I), early vertebrates learned by trial and error (part II), early mammals learned to simulate the world in imagination (part III), and early primates learned to model minds, including their own (part IV). Figure 1 puts the five together.

Figure 1. The five breakthroughs in Bennett’s account, the animals in which each first appeared, and the AI counterparts discussed in this series. Each breakthrough builds on the ones before it. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic summarizing Bennett (2023).

The fifth breakthrough is speaking. It is the one that most obviously connects to today’s AI, because the most capable AI systems we have are, at their core, models of language. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument, and some connections, notably to the data that children and language models learn from, come from the broader literature.

1. Breakthrough 5, Speaking: sharing what is in our heads

Many animals communicate. Vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for eagles, leopards and snakes, and apes can be taught hundreds of signs. What sets human language apart, in Bennett’s account, is what it carries. Thanks to the earlier breakthroughs, a human brain holds a rich inner simulation of the world and of other minds. Language lets one brain put part of that simulation into another: what happened at the river yesterday, how to shape a stone tool, who cannot be trusted.

That changes how learning works. Until now, every animal had to learn mostly from its own experience, plus whatever it could copy by watching. With language, a person can learn from the experience of people they have never met, including people who died long ago. Knowledge no longer has to be rediscovered in each generation; it can accumulate.

2. A perfect storm

Why did this happen in our lineage and not in other apes? Bennett describes an unlikely combination of pressures, each of which made the next more likely.

Out of the forest, into tools and meat

As African forests shrank and gave way to savannah, early humans moved into a new way of life: making stone tools and eating meat. Tool making is hard to learn and easy to lose. If a skill is passed on poorly, each generation does a little worse, and the technology never improves. Bennett argues that early proto-languages helped tool-making skills survive accurately from one generation to the next.

An experiment supports this idea. Researchers taught 184 modern volunteers to make simple stone flakes of the kind found at the oldest tool sites, passing the skill along chains of learners under five conditions, from examining finished flakes and watching an expert, to being taught by demonstration, with gestures or with speech (Morgan et al. 2015). Skill transmitted best when learners were taught, and best of all with spoken instruction; simply watching did little. The authors suggested that the very slow change of the oldest stone-tool tradition, which stayed much the same for roughly 700,000 years, may reflect how poorly skills spread without teaching and language.

A learning program, not a new brain part

Bennett argues that the brain did not need a new structure for language. Areas of the neocortex involved in language have counterparts in other primates. What changed, in his view, was a set of instincts that turns a child into a language learner: babies take part in back-and-forth “proto-conversations” with their caregivers long before they can speak, and they share attention with others, looking where someone points and pointing to show things themselves. Human infants begin to point to share interest at around their first birthday, a behavior that is rare or absent in other apes (Tomasello et al. 2007).

Together, joint attention and turn-taking work like a curriculum. When a parent and child look at the same thing and the parent names it, the child can tie the word to a part of its inner simulation of the world. Trained this way, older neocortical areas were repurposed for language.

Gossip, altruism and punishment

Once humans could talk, they began to talk with people who were not close kin, and much of what they talked about was other people. Robin Dunbar has argued that gossip is one of the main functions of language: it lets people keep track of who is reliable in groups too large to monitor directly (Dunbar 2004). Bennett describes a feedback loop. Language made it possible to reward people who helped others and to punish cheaters by spreading the word about them, which made cooperation with strangers safer, which made larger groups possible, which in turn favored people with better language skills.

Cooking and bigger brains

As groups grew and ideas began to hop from brain to brain, there was more to learn and remember, and bigger brains became worth their cost. The human brain is about three times the size of a chimpanzee’s, and brain tissue is expensive to run. Bennett points to cooking, a hypothesis developed by Richard Wrangham, as one way our ancestors paid for it: cooked food yields far more energy for less chewing and digestion (Wrangham 2009). Whether cooking drove brain growth or was made possible by it, it offered the surplus that a growing brain needed.

3. A mind tethered to other minds

From this perfect storm came the fifth and final breakthrough. Bennett’s closing point is that, with language, the human mind is no longer a single mind. Each of us is connected to others through a long history of accumulated ideas: tools, words, stories, mathematics and science, none of which any one of us could have invented alone. He also notes that language brought out both the best and the worst of us, from altruism toward strangers to coordinated cruelty.

For a scientist this is a familiar idea. No hydrologist derives the water balance, Darcy’s law or the Penman equation from scratch; we inherit them through textbooks and papers and add a little to the pile. Science is an unusually disciplined form of the accumulation that language made possible.

4. The AI connection: language without a body

Large language models are trained on exactly this accumulation: a large share of the text that humans have written down. In one sense they are the most direct AI counterpart of any breakthrough in the book. In another, they reverse the order in which evolution built intelligence.

Evolution built the inner simulation first and added language on top, so that words are labels for parts of a world model. Language models start from the words. Bennett discusses how early large language models produced fluent text while failing simple questions that require picturing a physical situation, and how newer models have closed many of these gaps. Whether they did so by building something like a world model from text, or by learning ever better statistical patterns in text about the world, is still debated. Some researchers argue that a system trained only on linguistic form cannot, in principle, learn meaning (Bender and Koller 2020).

The difference in how the two learn is easy to quantify (Figure 2). A child hears somewhere between a few million and a few tens of millions of words by age five, depending on how much language surrounds them. Even a 20-year-old who reads a great deal has met perhaps a few hundred million words. The training set of GPT-3 held about 500 billion tokens, and Llama 3 was trained on about 15 trillion (Frank 2023; Grattafiori et al. 2024). Frank (2023) suggests three possible reasons why children need so much less: a brain shaped by evolution before any data arrives, language grounded in sight, touch and action, and input that comes through social interaction in which the child takes part. These are, almost point for point, the earlier breakthroughs and the learning program described above.

Figure 2. Language heard or read by people compared with the training data of three language models, on a logarithmic scale. For people, the dark part of each bar shows the estimate for children growing up with little language around them and the light part extends to the estimate for language-rich environments (and, at age 20, heavy reading). Figure by Daeha Kim, based on estimates from Frank (2023) and training-set sizes reported by Frank (2023) and Grattafiori et al. (2024).

5. The correspondence at a glance

The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is.

Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close
Language as a way to share inner simulations Language models trained on human text Shared medium, reversed order
Accumulated knowledge across generations Pretraining on the written record Close match
Joint attention, naming what both can see Multimodal models linking words and images Partial match
Proto-conversations, learning by interaction Instruction tuning, learning from human feedback Partial match
Teaching skills with words Learning a task from instructions in a prompt Functional match
Small data, rich prior structure Huge data, weak prior structure Contrast

6. Closing: five breakthroughs and a sixth

Looking back over the series, each breakthrough solved a problem by building on the previous one. Steering needed a sense of good and bad; reinforcing used that sense to learn from experience; simulating let animals learn from experience they never had; mentalizing turned the simulator toward minds; and speaking let minds share their simulations, so that learning could continue beyond a single lifetime. Again and again, AI researchers have arrived at similar solutions, often without knowing that evolution had found them first.

The book ends by asking what a sixth breakthrough might be, and the obvious candidate is the one being built now: minds that are not made of neurons at all. If Bennett’s history teaches anything, it is that each new kind of intelligence was built from the parts of the old ones. It will be interesting to see which of the five our machines are still missing. I take up that question in part VI, the last post of this series.

Questions to think about

  1. Much of what a hydrologist knows was learned from papers and textbooks rather than from personal fieldwork. Which parts of your own expertise could not have been passed on in words?
  2. Morgan et al. found that stone-tool skills spread poorly by watching alone. Which skills in your field are still learned mainly by watching, and how could they be taught better?
  3. A child needs far less language than a language model. Which of Frank’s three explanations do you find most convincing, and how might it change how we train models?
